Today however, the "outsider" is likely to have professional qualifications of the highest order (otherwise the college would not be interested in hiring him) and to be acclimatized to the democratic processes of the secular or state university. And while no one expects total democracy on the academic scene, the scholar will be particularly sensitive to a line between first and second class citizenship drawn on any basis other than that of academic rank or professional achievement. In the above mentioned report of the Notre Dame Chapter of the American Association of University Professors, the basic outlook of the new breed of lay faculty emerges very clearly in the very statement of the problem as the members see it: "Even with the best of intentions he (the President of the university) is loath to delegate such authority and responsibility to a group the membership of which, considered (as it must be by him) in individual terms, is inhomogeneous, mortal and of extremely varying temperament, interests and capabilities.

message.content: Today, though, the "outsider" probably holds top professional qualifications (or the college would not want to hire him) and is used to the democratic procedures of secular and state universities. No one expects full democracy in academic life, but this scholar will notice and resent any division between first- and second-class faculty that rests on something other than academic rank or professional achievement. The Notre Dame Chapter of the American Association of University Professors, in the report cited earlier, shows how this new kind of lay faculty thinks in the way it states the problem: "Even with the best of intentions he (the President of the university) is loath to delegate such authority and responsibility to a group the membership of which, considered (as it must be by him) in individual terms, is inhomogeneous, mortal and of extremely varying temperament, interests and capabilities.
